episode_title: Building Bulletproof Real Estate Businesses: Diversification and Resilience with Shane Wilson

real_qa.q: How did Shane Wilson recover from bankruptcy after losing everything in the 2008 real estate crash?
real_qa.r: After going bankrupt with over a million dollars of debt in 2008, Shane got his real estate agent license in 2014 because he was afraid to take on debt again and not bankable after bankruptcy. He developed one of the first real estate teams in his area, which transferred his sales and marketing skills into a new income stream, and gradually rebuilt his business through diversification rather than focusing solely on house flipping.

real_qa.q: What is Shane Wilson's approach to building multiple income streams to protect against market downturns?
real_qa.r: Shane builds adjacent streams of income that fit within each business, like a giant corporation with different divisions. He operates a real estate investment division, a real estate agent team, a property management company (cash flow business), an insurance agency for landlords, and works as a HUD listing broker for foreclosures. He emphasizes that you focus on one thing, get it going well, then hire someone to cover 85-90% of things and move on to the next level, which fortifies the business for downturns and market cycles.
real_qa.requete: multiple income streams real estate diversification

real_qa.q: How many houses did Shane Wilson buy in 2007 and what was the outcome?
real_qa.r: In 2007 when he was 27 years old, Shane bought 27 houses, which he calls a massive mistake because the market continued down through 2011-2012 before flattening out. He went bankrupt as a result, citing his lack of knowledge, experience, arrogance, youth and ego as reasons he did not succeed—specifically because he was focused on only one skill set: buying and flipping houses.

real_qa.q: What does Shane Wilson say is the primary reason most real estate investors fail?
real_qa.r: Shane states that real estate does not have a lot of cash flow, and that is probably the biggest reason a lot of real estate investors and agents fail. When there is no underlying cash flow and you are over-leveraged, and the real income is not there to support you yet, or you do not have enough equity built up over the years, it becomes a very precarious situation if things go south.
real_qa.requete: why real estate investors fail cash flow

real_qa.q: How does Shane Wilson advise new real estate investors to find motivated sellers?
real_qa.r: Shane explains that a motivated seller is someone who has to sell their house even though they do not want to—they are moving, behind on payments, or have another reason to get rid of the property. To find them, you target foreclosure lists, divorce lists, and probate properties, then reach them through social media ads, door knocking, or direct mail, and craft a message to get them to respond using marketing and sales skills.
real_qa.requete: how to find motivated sellers real estate

real_qa.q: What key insight about making real estate deals did Shane Wilson learn from an attorney at a real estate group?
real_qa.r: An older attorney in his 70s stood up at a real estate group, held up a signed contract, and said: 'This is a deal. You know how I got this deal? I made an offer.' This made Shane realize that he can tell how many deals any real estate investor has or will do by the number of offers they make, and that most people do not find deals because they do not go out and make offers—it requires taking action.
real_qa.requete: real estate deals made by number of offers
